plan.topic: Scented cleaners + indoor ozone create billions of nanoparticles within minutes (Purdue, ACS Fall 2026)
plan.angle: That 'fresh clean' scent comes from terpenes such as limonene and pinene, including in 'natural' essential-oil cleaners. Indoors they react with ozone, and in Purdue's house tests the tiny particles formed could deliver a lung dose similar to standing by a busy road within about 20 minutes. Three fixes: choose fragrance-free products, run an exhaust fan while cleaning, and don't use ozone-generating 'air purifiers'. Say clearly: this is early conference data, and scientists are still working out the health effects.
plan.working_title: Your 'Clean' Smell Might Be Polluting Your Air
plan.why: Brand-new, low competition, and fits the ongoing 'toxins at home' interest. Easy fixes make it shareable. Wording must stay cautious because it isn't peer-reviewed yet. | fact-check: Verified: Purdue (Brandon Boor's team), presented at ACS Fall 2026 (23–27 Aug, 'Healthy Indoor Spaces' symposium). Terpenes from scented cleaners, both conventional and essential-oil-based, react with indoor ozone to form nanocluster aerosol (<3 nm). The estimate is 100 billion to 10 trillion particles deposited in the airways within 20 minutes, and the respiratory dose was comparable to or greater than standing by a busy road. Fixes: this is conference data, not a peer-reviewed paper. 'Billions' is accurate (the dose is to the lungs, not particles 'created'). The researchers' own advice is unscented products, running exhaust fans, and avoiding ozone-generating devices while cleaning. 'Open a window' can let more outdoor ozone in, so swap it for 'ventilate / run an exhaust fan'. Health effects of these particles are not established, so avoid fear language. Sources: https://www.acs.org/pressroom/presspacs/2026/august/scented-cleaning-products-create-invisible-air-pollution.html ; https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1139679 ; http://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260925093152.htm

social.instagram_caption:
That "fresh clean" smell might be polluting your air.

The scent often comes from terpenes, even in "natural" essential-oil cleaners.
Terpenes react with ozone that's already in your home and form invisible particles, mostly 1 to 30 nanometers wide.
In Purdue's test house, researchers measured billions to trillions of particles within minutes.
They estimate the particle dose reaching your lungs can be similar to standing by a busy road, or higher. The particles themselves are different, though.
The catch: these are small studies in one test house, and nobody has directly studied the health effects at everyday levels yet.

So no panic, just easy fixes 🪟
Keep cleaning. It removes germs.
Choose fragrance-free products.
Run an exhaust fan or open a window while you clean.
Don't run ozone-making gadgets like ozone "purifiers" while you clean.

Clean doesn't need a scent.

Save this for your next cleaning-aisle run, and share it with the person who loves a lemon-fresh spray.

factcheck.summary: Minor fixes applied after final review: s3; s5; s6

issues.claim: They react with indoor ozone, forming particles mostly 1 to 30 nanometers, missed by most home monitors.
issues.problem: None of the cited sources (ACS/EurekAlert release, ScienceDaily, Patra 2024) says these particles are 'missed by most home monitors'. It is probably true, since typical consumer PM2.5 sensors can't pick up particles that small, but it isn't sourced, and this pipeline has no human check before publishing.
issues.fix: Replace narration with: "They react with indoor ozone, forming tiny particles, mostly 1 to 30 nanometers wide. That's thousands of times thinner than a hair." (1–30 nm is at least ~2,000x thinner than a ~70,000 nm hair, so the comparison holds.) Or simply: "They react with indoor ozone, forming invisible particles, mostly 1 to 30 nanometers wide." Change the retention_device to drop the 'invisible to your monitor' hook.

issues.claim: nobody has measured the health effects of these particles at everyday levels yet
issues.problem: This absolute claim ('nobody has measured') is hard to verify. The sources only estimate exposure and dose and note possible effects such as irritation and inflammation; they don't prove there is no health data at all. Safer to hedge.
issues.fix: Replace narration with: "Here's the catch: these are small studies in one test house, and the health effects of these particles at everyday levels haven't been directly studied yet. So no panic, just easy fixes."

issues.claim: Go fragrance-free. Run an exhaust fan or open a window. And skip gadgets that make ozone, like ozone 'purifiers', especially while you clean.
issues.problem: The advice is accurate and matches the sources. The researchers mention far UV-C lamps as an example of an ozone-generating device, and the ScienceDaily and Phys.org write-ups stress that cleaning still removes germs. Without that line, some viewers could take the message as 'clean less'.
issues.fix: Replace narration with: "Keep cleaning, it removes germs. Just go fragrance-free, run an exhaust fan or open a window, and skip ozone-making gadgets like ozone 'purifiers' while you clean."
